intro: The second movement sets urgent A-minor music against memories of the funeral march. A brass chorale offers D major before the ending withdraws from that possibility.
question: How can a major-key arrival be a promise rather than an ending?

sections.mNote: running bass figures and sharp orchestral attacks

sections.label: Funeral-march memory

sections.label: The storm returns
sections.mNote: fast gestures briefly recover their force

sections.label: Low-register reflection

cues.title: A bass line launches the storm
cues.text: Bassoons, cellos and double basses set the opening in motion. Sharp upper attacks cross their running figure; the urgency comes from the opposition between these layers, not simply from everyone playing the same rhythm.
cues.evidence: Peters score, plate 9015, p. 48, shows the running lower parts and accented orchestral chords. The report rises from the quiet file opening into active 0:05–0:35 windows; no exact instrumental entry is timed.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Leaps against running notes
cues.text: Listen for short, upward-leaping gestures against the continuous smaller notes. Mahler can keep those gestures recognisable while changing their register, accompaniment and the length of the phrase around them.
cues.evidence: The opening score and Lew Smoley’s guide identify the rising leaps and running figure. The report sustains relatively high levels through 0:15–1:15: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-2-sturmisch-bewegt-mit-groster-vehemenz/.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening suddenly loses weight
cues.text: The first rush retreats into a much quieter region. Listen through the reduction: the thinning sound prepares a change in the kind of movement, from rapid figures towards a slower melodic line.
cues.evidence: The report marks a strong boundary at 1:20; relative level falls from −14.5 dB at 1:15 to −41.2 at 1:25, before recovering gradually. Peters pp. 57–58 supply the following written tempo change.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The preceding march remembered
cues.text: Mahler explicitly asks for the tempo of the first movement’s funeral march. The cello melody is not an unrelated slow interlude: the Fifth carries earlier material across its movement boundary.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 58, rehearsal 5: Bedeutend langsamer, im Tempo des ersten Satzes “Trauermarsch”, with cellos cantando. The 1:36 boundary and quiet 1:35–2:25 span anchor the passage approximately.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two summers, changing circumstances
cues.text: Mahler begins the Fifth in 1901 and completes its composition the following summer. Between those summers he meets Alma Schindler and marries her. The chronology is clear; a detailed marital story assigned to this movement is not.
cues.evidence: Composition and family chronology: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/. No biographical interpretation of a timed musical event is proposed.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Fast gestures reassert themselves
cues.text: The opening’s active material returns before the slow melody can become a stable alternative. Listen for the contrast between a renewed attack and the longer, quieter continuation that follows it.
cues.evidence: The report marks 3:14 and rises to −11.2 dB at 3:25, then shows another major retreat at 4:06–4:10. Smoley describes the abbreviated return of the opening material between slow spans.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another abrupt reduction
cues.text: A forceful phrase gives way to a much lighter sound. Compare this withdrawal with the one after the opening: repeated changes of scale prevent the movement from behaving like one continuous crescendo.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 4:06 and 4:10 coincide with a fall from −14.9 dB at 4:00 to −39.8 at 4:15. The following low-level region lasts far longer than a single pause.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A low line has space
cues.text: In the central slow span, the lower-string melody has much more space around it. Listen for the difference between a melody exposed by fewer competing parts and one projected by increased volume.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s account describes the extended cello arioso over a sparse pedal texture. The report’s 4:15–5:10 windows remain quiet and low in spectral brightness; it does not identify the instrument independently.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Accompaniment slowly returns
cues.text: As the reflective stretch expands, attend to the support around the melody. A held note, a repeated pulse and a moving counterline do different jobs, even when they occupy the same low register.
cues.evidence: The movement guide describes the cello line acquiring accompanying parts. The report shows a gradual recovery in level from 4:25 through 5:35; the note avoids assigning an exact entrance to any desk.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A symphony without a text
cues.text: The Fifth begins Mahler’s group of three entirely instrumental middle symphonies. Unlike the Second, Third and Fourth, it supplies no sung words to guide the listener’s interpretation of a march, a dance or a chorale.
cues.evidence: The all-instrumental Fifth–Seventh grouping and contrast with earlier vocal symphonies: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A quieter turning region
cues.text: The central span loses force again before the faster music gathers momentum. Listen for the way the dynamic contour resets: the next rise must be built from a reduced starting point.
cues.evidence: The report marks 6:38, 7:02 and 7:08. Relative level falls to −31.2 dB at 6:40 and stays comparatively low through 7:10 before increasing after 7:20.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The motifs change partners
cues.text: The renewed active span develops earlier gestures rather than introducing a wholly separate movement. Follow a short rhythmic shape as its surroundings change: a theme can retain its identity without retaining its original accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s guide describes the developmental recombination of the movement’s themes. The 7:20 boundary and increasing activity through 7:25–8:25 provide a broad anchor, not a bar-exact formal division.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Two kinds of forward motion
cues.text: Separate the fast repeated activity from the longer melodic line it supports. When both are active, the smaller notes can intensify a phrase without replacing it as the music’s main shape.
cues.evidence: The score’s recurrent running figures and extended themes underpin this listening task. The report records dense activity around 8:05–8:30; no machine onset estimate is treated as a count of written notes.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Published, then revised
cues.text: Peters first publishes the Fifth in 1904. Mahler continues revising its orchestration afterwards, including during his final years. A printed score is therefore a specific version, not an automatic record of every performance’s choices.
cues.evidence: Publication and revision history: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-history/. The edition used by this Peabody performance is not established.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A forceful crest, then another turn
cues.text: The renewed storm reaches another concentrated surge and then changes direction. Resist treating each loud arrival as the movement’s destination: Mahler still has a different kind of broad statement in reserve.
cues.evidence: A strong 9:22 boundary precedes the −9.0 dB window at 9:25; the level later falls to −26.5 at 9:55. The future chorale is established by the score, not predicted from the trace.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Recognising material through change
cues.text: Listen for familiar rising and falling gestures inside the accumulating texture. Development need not hide its themes: it changes their scale, combinations and harmonic surroundings while leaving enough of their outline to recognise.
cues.evidence: The movement guide traces the recurrence and combination of opening and march-derived motifs. The broad 9:45–10:35 span alternates quieter and forceful windows; no exact thematic entry is assigned.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The approach keeps moving
cues.text: Before the broad chorale, the music remains active rather than clearing a completely silent space. Listen for the relationship between an arriving melody and the motion that continues beneath it.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 102 shows active strings beneath the brass chorale. The report remains forceful through 10:35–11:10, before the 11:16 boundary; the note describes the approach as a region.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Brass chords in D major
cues.text: The chorale presents a broad, chordal brass statement against moving strings and harp. D major offers a different tonal destination from the movement’s A-minor opening, but it will not yet provide the symphony’s final ending.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 102 and the movement guide establish the D-major brass chorale and accompaniment. The 11:16 boundary, high levels and sustained D-major estimates at 11:15–11:30 support the approximate passage; the score establishes the key.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Breadth above restless accompaniment
cues.text: Keep the brass’s longer values separate from the quicker string motion. A chorale can sound broad without making every instrumental layer slow; Mahler preserves energy underneath the apparent arrival.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 102 shows the layered rhythms, with the chorale extending into the following pages. The report’s forceful 11:55–12:05 region precedes the marked reduction at 12:15–12:20; this is a passage-level comparison.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The promise does not hold
cues.text: After the chorale subsides, the faster gestures return. The major-key arrival has been an episode within the movement, not its permanent solution; the closing music must work through the interruption once more.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 107 shows the reduction after the chorale; Smoley describes the return of opening fragments. The report falls to −29.5 dB at 12:20 and rises through 12:30–12:55, locating the broad join.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fragments instead of a full statement
cues.text: In the final pages, isolated figures and a delicate high texture replace the earlier massed attacks. Listen for the spaces around the remaining sounds, rather than waiting for another complete chorale.
cues.evidence: Peters p. 116 shows a light high-string texture, wind fragments and isolated harp notes. The report falls after 13:00, marks 13:16 and stays quiet through the end. Exact instrument entrances are not timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Running figures yield to a cello melody
transitions.how: The fast woodwind figures diminish and the texture opens out over a timpani roll. Mahler explicitly restores the first movement’s funeral-march tempo. Cellos take a sustained melody in the F-minor region, with bass punctuation and sparse wind responses replacing the opening’s crowded attacks. The slower music recalls the earlier march rather than establishing an unrelated interlude.
transitions.evidence: Peters pp. 57–58 document the thinning and slower cello passage. The 1:20 level collapse and 1:36 boundary locate the transition broadly; the score and Smoley’s account supply the F-minor context.

transitions.title: Short gestures displace the long line
transitions.how: The long melodic span gives way to the opening’s shorter, more forceful gestures and running accompaniment. The faster material is abbreviated: its purpose here is to reassert the opposition between storm and march, not to repeat the entire opening intact.
transitions.evidence: Smoley describes the abbreviated return of the fast material. The report’s 3:14 boundary, rise to the 3:25 crest and denser 3:35–3:45 windows support this approximate join.

transitions.title: The orchestral attack leaves a sparse line
transitions.how: Instead of carrying the renewed storm straight into another climax, Mahler strips away much of its accompaniment. A long cello-led span unfolds above a sparse pedal texture, extending the slow material into something closer to an arioso. Sustained support replaces the running bass’s propulsion, and the later growth begins from that reduced texture.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s guide describes the cello arioso and pedal support. The 4:06–4:10 boundaries and fall from −14.9 dB at 4:00 to −39.8 at 4:15 anchor the broad reduction; no individual cello entry is asserted.

transitions.title: The isolated ideas enter a denser argument
transitions.how: The reflective music fragments and the faster gestures recover momentum. Mahler brings previously opposed ideas into closer contact: brief rising figures, running accompaniment and longer lines become material for changing combinations. Increasing activity and a thicker orchestral texture make the join audible without requiring a completely new theme.
transitions.evidence: The developmental process is described in Smoley’s guide. The report’s 7:02, 7:08 and 7:20 boundaries and rising activity after 7:20 place a broad turning region, not a uniquely determined formal bar.

transitions.title: Broad brass chords crown the moving texture
transitions.how: The active writing opens onto a D-major chorale in the brass. Mahler does not discard the preceding motion: string scales and arpeggiated figures, reinforced by harp, continue beneath the longer chordal statements. The join changes the balance between melodic breadth and accompaniment, making D major sound like an arrival while preserving the energy that carried the music towards it.
transitions.evidence: Peters p. 102 establishes the key and layered scoring. The 11:16 boundary and strong 11:15–11:30 windows provide the recording anchor; chroma supports but does not establish the harmonic identification.

transitions.title: The broad arrival gives way again
transitions.how: The brass statement diminishes into a slower, thinner passage. Fragments of the storm then re-enter, with renewed short attacks and running motion. This prevents the D-major chorale from functioning as the final answer: the movement ends only after another surge has itself dissolved into sparse strings, winds and harp.
transitions.evidence: Peters p. 107 shows the chorale’s reduction and p. 116 the later sparse coda. The report falls steeply at 12:15–12:20, then rebuilds from 12:25 to 12:55; the marker is a passage estimate.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, II, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed pp. 48, 57–58, 102, 107, 116. Broad scoring snapshots around audio-feature changes, not bar-aligned entries. The performance’s edition is unidentified.

timeline.note: Opening-page span, p. 48: running lower parts oppose short orchestral attacks; parts join successively, not all on the first note.
Transition passage, p. 57: diminishing wind figures over sustained support; approximate placement at the 1:20 reduction.
Slow passage, p. 58: cellos cantando, bass punctuation, sparse winds and sustained support; placed around the 1:36 change.
Chorale passage, p. 102: broad brass above moving strings and harp; the 11:16 boundary gives approximate placement.
Post-chorale reduction, p. 107: sustained brass and low instruments diminish; broad placement near the 12:15 retreat.
Late coda, p. 116: light upper-string texture, wind fragments and isolated harp notes, appearing intermittently rather than as a continuous ensemble.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
